column3: The throne borne by angels gives a distinct cosmic-throne frame, setting the queen's great throne beneath a higher order of sovereignty.
A woman made a sign with her son is only a broad female-figure resonance and does not illuminate her rule, resources, or throne.
It directly questions who receives a share of dominion, closely clarifying the focus's description of a woman who rules her people.
Its great event shares the adjective great but concerns the Hour's earthquake rather than the queen's great throne.
Solomon's demand for submission develops the political encounter introduced by the report of the ruling queen.
God's dominion over heavens and earth, together with power over all things, provides the decisive frame for the queen's limited rule and abundance.
The fixed term of destroyed towns does not materially clarify the queen, her rule, or her throne.
Following unpaid guides is unrelated to the report of a woman sovereign with a great throne.
Naming God King of mankind supplies a compact divine-sovereignty counterpart to the queen's human rule.
God gives and removes dominion at will, directly relativizing the authority and wealth attributed to the queen.
The surah's opening promise of guidance and good news does not specifically develop this political report.
God as Lord of the great Throne directly re-scales the queen's great throne within the immediately ensuing account.
Its marital reconciliation setting and reference to a woman do not illuminate a female monarch or her throne.
The challenge about the promised event adds no useful link to the queen's rule or possessions.
God as Lord of the Throne and the rejection of competing gods provide a theological counterpart, though less direct than 27:26.
The scene of two women at a well offers a distant contrast in women's social position, not a close parallel to female sovereignty.
Solomon's decision to test the hoopoe's report is the immediate verification step for the focus's claim about the queen.
Great success as divine favor does not clarify the queen's great throne.
The warning of a great day's punishment shares only the adjective great and remains contextually separate.
Revelation exposing what was concealed does not develop the queen's political status or throne.
Its condemnation of great wrongdoing is a theological contrast to the following account's sun worship, but it does not clarify the focus itself.
Fear of a great day's punishment shares a formulaic adjective but not the focus's rulership or throne imagery.
The queen's final recognition of her wrongdoing and submission completes the transformation initiated by the report of her sovereignty.
Angels carrying the Throne give a significant divine-throne contrast and also connect throne imagery with God's comprehensive mercy and knowledge.
The passage on distorted judgment and punishment has no material bearing on the queen's rule or great throne.
Its warning about false worship is too general to add to the specific report of the queen and her court.
A great share granted to the patient does not clarify the queen's throne or political authority.
Inheritance allocations involving a woman do not illuminate the focus's monarch or her possessions.
The plot against Salih and his household is local-surah material but unrelated to the queen's royal scene.
Undivided divine dominion and creation in measure provide a broad theological counterpoint to the queen's earthly rule and resources.
Moses' promise of patience and obedience does not clarify the focus.
The sudden inability to make a will or return home has no useful connection to the queen's sovereignty.
It directly asks who will bring her throne before she arrives in submission, turning the focus's defining possession into the next narrative action.
The ruined town on its roofs contrasts collapse with the focus's flourishing royal structure, but the lexical overlap is not the same throne image.
The opening description of believers' worship does not specifically develop the queen's report.
A great dominion in paradise is a distant eschatological counterpart to the queen's great earthly throne.
The demand that each person receive open scrolls does not clarify the focus.
Human ownership of livestock offers only a broad possession parallel, without rulership or throne imagery.
God's dominion over heavens and earth supplies a useful higher-sovereignty frame, though it repeats the point already made by nearer dominion verses.
Angels surrounding the Throne portray the divine court, a meaningful contrast to the queen's visible royal throne.
The immediately following verse identifies the queen and her people as sun worshippers, explaining the religious condition of the polity described in the focus.
A sacred object carried by angels serves as a sign of kingship, offering a limited comparison to a throne as royal sign.
Family reunion and individual responsibility do not clarify the queen's rule, wealth, or throne.
The instruction to consult those with knowledge is unrelated to the focus's royal report.
The Merciful established over the Throne gives a concise divine-throne counterpart to the queen's great throne.
The prophet's lack of refuge apart from God does not illuminate the queen's political situation.
The later statement about those unable to hear guidance is too general to clarify the focus.
David receiving kingship and wisdom gives a distant model of God-given rule, but its military setting differs from the queen's court.
God as the true King and Lord of the noble Throne clearly contrasts ultimate sovereignty with the queen's temporal rule.
Mountains and paths enabling guidance do not materially clarify the queen's rule or throne.
Israel's request for a king introduces political leadership, but the subsequent military test is only loosely comparable.
Moses seeing a fire and seeking guidance has no connection to the focus's royal report.
Universal humbled arrival on the Day of the Trumpet broadly contrasts with earthly rule, but adds little to the focus.
Talut's appointment shows that kingship is bestowed by God rather than secured by wealth, a useful contrast to the queen's evident abundance.
The prophet's fear of a great day's punishment shares only formulaic language and does not illuminate the queen's throne.
God's dominion over all realms and power over all things provide another broad corrective to any absolute reading of the queen's authority.
God's establishment over the Throne and knowledge of all movement provide a substantial divine-throne frame beyond the queen's local rule.
The possible removal of revelation does not clarify the queen, her people, or her throne.
Moses' call and blessing in the fire do not specifically develop the focus's royal report.
God as Lord of heavens, earth, and the Throne rejects false descriptions and provides a theological contrast to the queen's sun worship.
The queen is asked whether the altered throne is hers, directly testing the identity and significance of the throne first described in the focus.
Being heedless amid delusion does not materially clarify the queen's report.
Great divine bounty is too general to explain the queen's abundance or throne.
Solomon orders the queen's throne altered in order to test her guidance, directly developing the great throne named in the focus.
Creation, restoration, and provision challenge rival gods, supplying broad theological context for the account's critique of sun worship.
Abraham exposes a ruler's claim to life-and-death power, sharply distinguishing human kingship from divine control in a way relevant to the queen's rule.
Dhu al-Qarnayn is established in the land and given means for everything, closely paralleling the focus's account of a ruler granted from every thing.
Truthfulness and piety do not clarify the queen's sovereignty or throne.
Judgment-day dominion belongs to God, giving an eschatological limit to the queen's present earthly rule.
Solomon's inheritance and being given from every thing directly parallel the focus's claim that the queen was given from every thing, setting the two rulers in comparison.
The inability of the dead and deaf to hear is not a specific continuation of the queen's royal scene.
The question naming God as Lord of the seven heavens and great Throne gives a direct divine-throne counterpart, though already substantially covered.
God's encompassing knowledge and numbering of all things lightly echoes the focus's phrase about being given from every thing.
One God and the arrogance of deniers provide general theological background to the queen's people's idolatry, not her rule or throne.
Solomon's prayer for an unmatched dominion directly relates to the royal comparison that the focus opens, while keeping his rule as a divine gift.
The immediately preceding verse introduces the hoopoe's certain news from Saba, making the focus the content of that report.
God answers the distressed and makes successors on earth, offering only a broad sovereignty contrast to the queen's earthly rule.
The glorious Throne provides a concise divine-throne resonance but adds little beyond earlier throne passages.
Zachariah's question about having a son with an infertile wife does not clarify a woman ruler.
Ritual restrictions and ethical cooperation do not materially clarify the focus.
Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion and who has power over all things, a compact higher-sovereignty frame for the queen's rule and resources.
Those distributing a command do not clarify the queen's throne or authority.
God's ordering of earth, rivers, mountains, and seas supplies broad theological context against the queen's people's false worship.
Trust in God as Lord of the great Throne supplies a direct divine-throne counterpart, though it is redundant with closer throne parallels.
God granting Moses' request does not clarify the queen's royal status or possessions.
The marital-law formulation using possession is unrelated to the focus's political rule.
God's dominion over heavens and earth and power over life and death provide a further broad limit on human sovereignty.
The guarded heaven scene does not clarify the queen's rule or throne.
Affirming the Day of Judgment does not materially illuminate the focus.
God's dominion over heavens, earth, and what lies between them joins sovereignty with return and judgment, broadening the contrast to earthly kingship.
The creation and resurrection sequence does not specifically clarify the queen, her resources, or her throne.
On the day all are exposed, dominion belongs to God alone, giving a clear eschatological corrective to the queen's present rule.
Inheritance shares do not illuminate the focus's woman sovereign or her great throne.
The human life-cycle account does not clarify the focus.
Remembering the reminder at will does not develop the queen's report.
Human growth from earth does not materially illuminate the focus.
Objects invoked apart from God create nothing and are created, providing limited theological context for the following sun-worship diagnosis.
The oath procedure's fifth invocation of wrath is unrelated to the queen's rule or throne.
Private deliberation and calculation do not clarify the focus.
Denying the Day of Judgment does not materially illuminate the queen's royal report.
The immediately following diagnosis of their failure to prostrate to God completes the religious error introduced by the focus's report of the queen and her people.
Solomon orders the letter delivered and awaits the response, beginning the diplomatic exchange prompted by the report of the queen's kingdom.
The queen convenes her chiefs after receiving a noble letter, directly displaying her authority and courtly decision-making.
The letter's divine invocation identifies Solomon's authority, but it adds less to the focus than the queen's ensuing political response.
The queen asks her chiefs for counsel while retaining the final decision, directly depicting the exercise of the rule reported in the focus.
Her chiefs affirm military strength but defer the command to her, clarifying the resources and authority of her kingdom.
The queen's observation that kings devastate cities and abase their honored people gives an explicit political account of the power she herself possesses.
Her decision to send a gift shows diplomacy and material resources as instruments of rule, developing the focus's statement that she was given from every thing.
Solomon's rejection of material enrichment directly contrasts divine gift with the queen's display of wealth and tests the limits of her diplomatic strategy.
Solomon's threat of force and expulsion advances the confrontation between his divinely grounded rule and the queen's earthly kingdom.
The ifrit's offer to bring her throne directly treats the throne named in the focus as a movable sign of royal power.
The throne is brought before Solomon's glance returns, and he calls it a test of divine bounty; this is the fullest reinterpretation of the focus's great throne.
What she had worshipped apart from God had barred the queen, directly explaining the religious condition first stated just after the focus.
The sign given to Saba in its settled land supplies broader context for the polity from which the queen and her abundant kingdom are reported.
Saba's later loss of its flourishing gardens provides a consequential contrast to the focus's picture of royal abundance and stability.
Joseph raises his parents upon a throne, providing a close literal throne parallel in a different scene of political elevation and family honor.
God strengthened David's kingdom and gave him wisdom and decisive speech, offering a close model of divinely enabled royal capacity.
Solomon's testing through what was placed upon his throne presents another direct throne scene in which royal power is shown to be contingent.
Pharaoh's claim to Egypt's dominion and flowing rivers gives a sharp contrastive example of a ruler publicly asserting territorial wealth and authority.
The promise of succession and established religion supplies a broad theology of secure rule, but not the focus's specific queen-and-throne scene.
